Background & Epidemiology.title: Background & Epidemiology
Background & Epidemiology.html:
Not every patient on a radiation service has a cancer you are trying to cure. A large share of the day is palliative work (pain, bleeding, obstruction, a spine that is about to fail), emergencies paged in overnight, and a smaller group of benign conditions where low doses of radiation calm inflammation or stop tissue from overgrowing. This module is the catch-all for that work, plus a short tour of the sites the other modules don't cover.

There is no anatomy, nodal, or staging reading here. The question that replaces staging is: what is the goal, how long is this patient likely to live, and what is the least burdensome treatment that reaches that goal?

Four Kinds of Patients

PatientTypical exampleWhat radiation is forTypical dose range
PalliativePainful bone metastasis, bleeding bladder tumor, obstructing lung massRelieve a symptom or prevent one, with as few visits as possible8 Gy in 1 to 30 Gy in 10
EmergencyCord compression, SVC obstruction, life-threatening bleedingProtect function (walking, breathing) or stop the event, fast8 Gy in 1 to 30 Gy in 10, started within hours to a day
BenignKnee osteoarthritis, Dupuytren nodules, keloid, before a hip replacementCalm inflammation or stop overgrowth when other treatment has failedA few Gy (inflammation) to about 30 Gy (overgrowth)
Functional or vascular SRSTrigeminal neuralgia, arteriovenous malformationA precise single high dose to a tiny targetAbout 16-25 Gy to an AVM margin; 70-90 Gy maximum to the trigeminal nerve
The dose depends on the goal: a few Gy calms inflammation, 8-30 Gy relieves symptoms, 50-80 Gy cures cancer, and a single very high dose to a tiny target destroys it.

Palliative Radiation: Who and Why

Palliative radiation is one of the most common things a radiation oncologist does; a large share of all radiation courses are given with palliative intent. The most common reason by far is a painful bone metastasis.

1
Pain

Bone metastases, nerve or plexus invasion, liver capsule stretch, pelvic masses. Pain relief usually starts within 1-2 weeks and peaks at about 4-6 weeks.

2
Bleeding

Hemoptysis, hematuria, vaginal or rectal bleeding, fungating skin or breast tumors. Hemostatic RT often slows bleeding within days.

3
Obstruction

Airway, esophagus, SVC, ureter, or bowel. Stents act faster; radiation can be more durable.

4
Neurologic function

Cord compression and brain metastases. The goal is to keep the patient walking, thinking, and continent.

Which Cancers Go to Bone?

Five primaries account for most bone metastases: prostate, breast, lung, kidney, and thyroid, plus multiple myeloma, which lives in the marrow. The axial skeleton (spine, pelvis, ribs) and the proximal femur and humerus are the usual sites, because that is where red marrow is.

Lesion typeTypical cancersWhy it matters
Blastic (bone-forming, bright on CT)Prostate, some breastShows up well on bone scan; less likely to fracture
Lytic (bone-destroying, dark on CT)Kidney, thyroid, myeloma, lung, many breastHigher fracture risk; myeloma can be invisible on bone scan
MixedBreast, lungJudge by the lytic component
Clinical Pearl

Most patients with bone metastases have them in more than one place. Treat the lesion that is causing the symptom, not every spot on the scan, unless there is a specific reason (see prophylactic radiation in Palliative Radiation).

Benign Disease: Who and Why

Radiation for benign conditions is common in Germany and other parts of Europe and much less common in the United States, but you will still see it, and it shows up on exams. It works through two mechanisms:

A few Gy
Anti-inflammatory

Very low doses (often 0.5-1 Gy per fraction) change how macrophages, white cells, and blood vessel walls behave in inflamed tissue. Used for painful osteoarthritis, plantar fasciitis, and other degenerative joint and tendon problems.

Roughly 7-30 Gy
Anti-proliferative

Moderate doses stop fibroblasts or bone-forming precursor cells from multiplying. Used for Dupuytren and Ledderhose disease, keloids, heterotopic ossification, and gynecomastia prevention.

Functional and vascular radiosurgery (trigeminal neuralgia, AVMs) is a third group: the target is tiny and the single dose is very high. It gets its own reading.

The Rule for Benign Radiation

1
Other options first

Radiation is usually offered after conservative treatment (drugs, injections, physical therapy) fails or isn't tolerated.

2
Lowest effective dose

Benign doses are a small fraction of cancer doses, to the smallest volume that works.

3
Respect the cancer risk

Any radiation carries a small lifetime risk of a second cancer. Be cautious in young patients and near the thyroid, breast, and gonads, and say so during consent.

The Rest of the Service

Lymphoma, skin cancer, sarcoma, plasmacytoma and myeloma, pediatric tumors, total body irradiation, and a few smaller sites (bladder, seminoma, thymoma, eye) don't have their own module. The last reading covers each in a few lines: what it is, where radiation fits, and the trial or rule you're most likely to be asked about.

High-Yield Summary
  • This service sees four kinds of patients: palliative, emergency, benign, and functional or vascular radiosurgery, and each uses a very different dose.
  • A painful bone metastasis is the most common reason for palliative radiation, and prostate, breast, lung, kidney, and thyroid cancer and myeloma are the usual sources.
  • Pain relief after palliative radiation usually starts in 1 to 2 weeks and peaks at about 4 to 6 weeks.
  • Benign conditions are treated either with a few Gy to calm inflammation or with moderate doses to stop tissue from overgrowing.
  • Benign radiation is offered after other treatments fail, at the lowest effective dose, with honest consent about the small lifetime cancer risk, especially in young patients.

Workup & Prognosis.title: Workup & Prognosis
Workup & Prognosis.html:
In a curative site, stage tells you the plan. On the palliative service, five questions do that job. Answer them in order on every consult:

1
What is the symptom, and is it from this lesion?

A painful spot on the bone scan may not be the cause of the pain. Match the exam to the imaging.

2
What is the goal?

Relieve pain, stop bleeding, keep walking, prevent a fracture, or durable control of limited disease.

3
How long is the patient likely to live?

Prognosis picks the fractionation: weeks, months, or years.

4
Is the bone or spine stable, and is the cord safe?

Instability and cord compression may need a surgeon before (or instead of) radiation.

5
What has already been treated?

Prior radiation to the same area limits what you can safely give now.

Stage tells you the plan in curative disease. In palliative disease, the goal, the prognosis, and stability tell you the plan.

Goals and Prognosis

Start with what matters to the patient and what they understand about their illness. Then estimate prognosis honestly. Clinicians tend to overestimate how long patients will live, which leads to courses that are longer than the patient's remaining time.

Expected survivalWhat it means for radiation
WeeksSingle fraction (8 Gy in 1) or no radiation; focus on hospice and comfort. Pain relief takes 1-2 weeks to start, so very short survival may not leave time to benefit.
MonthsShort courses (8 Gy in 1 or 20 Gy in 5). Accept a higher chance of needing retreatment for fewer visits.
Years (or limited disease)Longer courses (30 Gy in 10) or SBRT for durable local control and less retreatment.

What Predicts Survival

  • Performance status (KPS or ECOG) is the single most useful predictor. A patient in bed most of the day (KPS 40 or less, ECOG 3-4) usually has weeks to a few months.
  • Primary cancer: breast and prostate cancer with bone-only disease can live for years; lung cancer with visceral metastases usually much less.
  • Where the metastases are: bone only is better than liver or brain.
  • Systemic options left: a patient starting effective targeted therapy has a different outlook from one who has exhausted treatment.
Reference: prognostic scores you might hear named▾
  • Chow three-item score: non-breast primary, metastases beyond bone, and KPS 60 or less. Median survival falls from more than a year with 0-1 factors to about 2 months with all 3.
  • TEACHH: tumor type, ECOG, age, prior palliative chemo, hospitalizations in the last 3 months, and liver metastases.
  • Rades score (cord compression) and the GPA (brain metastases, see CNS).
  • The surprise question ("Would I be surprised if this patient died in the next year?") is a quick bedside screen for a goals-of-care talk.

Imaging: Which Test Answers Which Question

QuestionBest testWhy
Where are the bone metastases?Bone scan or PET/CT (FDG; PSMA for prostate)Bone scan sees bone-forming activity, so it can miss purely lytic lesions such as myeloma (use a skeletal survey, low-dose CT, or MRI)
Will this long bone break?Plain X-rays of the whole bone, then CTX-rays show cortical destruction; a lytic lesion is visible only after a large share of the bone is gone
Is the cord compressed?MRI of the whole spineMany patients have disease at more than one level; CT myelogram if MRI is impossible
Is the spine stable?CT plus MRIBony collapse, alignment, and which parts of the vertebra are involved feed the SINS score
PlanningCT simulationOld plans and diagnostic imaging are fused to see prior dose and the target

Do you need a biopsy? Yes if there is no known cancer, if this would be the first metastasis, if the lesion is solitary after a long disease-free interval, or if a second cancer, lymphoma, myeloma, or infection is possible. A diagnosis of lymphoma or myeloma changes the plan, because both are very radiosensitive and often treated with drugs first.

Is the Spine Stable? SINS

The Spinal Instability Neoplastic Score (SINS) adds six features into a 0-18 score. You don't need to memorize the points; you need to know what pushes a spine toward instability and that a score of 7 or higher means a spine surgeon should see the patient.

  • 0-6: stable. Radiation alone is reasonable from a stability standpoint.
  • 7-12: potentially unstable. Surgical consultation.
  • 13-18: unstable. Stabilization is usually needed; radiation does not fix a broken spine.
Clinical Pearl

Mechanical pain (pain with movement, sitting up, or bearing weight that is relieved by lying still) suggests instability. Biologic pain (worse at night, steady, relieved by steroids) comes from the tumor itself and responds to radiation.

Is the Cord Compressed? Bilsky Grade

The Bilsky epidural spinal cord compression (ESCC) grade describes on axial T2 MRI how far tumor has pushed into the canal.

GradeWhat MRI showsWhat it means
0Tumor in bone onlyLow grade
1a-1cEpidural tumor that touches or indents the thecal sac but does not deform the cordLow grade: usually radiation (conventional or SBRT)
2Cord compressed, but CSF still visible around itHigh grade
3Cord compressed with no CSF visibleHigh grade: surgical decompression if the tumor is radioresistant and the patient can tolerate it

Putting It Together: NOMS

Spine teams combine these into the NOMS framework, four questions that decide surgery, conventional RT, or SBRT:

LetterQuestion
NeurologicHow high is the Bilsky grade, and is there myelopathy or radiculopathy?
OncologicIs the tumor radiosensitive (lymphoma, myeloma, seminoma, breast, prostate, small cell) or radioresistant to conventional doses (kidney, thyroid, melanoma, sarcoma, colon, liver, many NSCLC)?
MechanicalIs the spine unstable (SINS)?
SystemicCan the patient tolerate surgery, and what is the prognosis?
Radiosensitive tumors usually get conventional RT even with high-grade compression. Radioresistant tumors with low-grade compression can get SBRT; with high-grade compression they often need surgery first.

Will This Long Bone Break? Mirels Score

For a lesion in the femur, humerus, or another long bone, Mirels' score adds four features (site, pain, lesion type, and how much of the bone's width is involved), each scored 1-3, for a total of 4-12.

  • 9 or more: high fracture risk. Orthopedics for prophylactic fixation, then postoperative radiation.
  • 8: borderline; use judgment.
  • 7 or less: radiation alone is reasonable.
Clinical Pearl

Pain with weight bearing (functional pain) in a lytic femur lesion is a warning sign of impending fracture. Ask about it on every bone metastasis consult and keep the patient off the leg until orthopedics weighs in.

Prior Radiation

Always ask whether the patient has had radiation before. Get the old plan, find the previous dose to the spinal cord or other limiting organs, and add it to what you plan now. Re-irradiation is often possible, especially with conventional palliative doses or SBRT, but it is planned around the cumulative dose.

A man with prostate cancer has a painful L3 metastasis. Pain is worst at night, steady, and better on dexamethasone. MRI shows bone disease without epidural extension. Biologic or mechanical pain?

Biologic. Night pain that steroids relieve comes from the tumor and usually responds well to radiation.

A woman with renal cell carcinoma has back pain only when she sits up or stands. CT shows a lytic T12 lesion with 60% collapse. What score do you calculate and who do you call?

SINS, which will be in at least the indeterminate range (junctional level, mechanical pain, lytic lesion, collapse over 50%). Call spine surgery: mechanical pain suggests instability, which radiation can't fix.

A lytic lesion in the mid femoral shaft takes up most of the bone's width and hurts with walking. Mirels score?

Lower limb 2 + functional pain 3 + lytic 3 + more than 2/3 of the width 3 = 11. High fracture risk: orthopedics for prophylactic fixation, then postoperative RT.

A patient with myeloma has new rib pain but a negative bone scan. What do you do?

Bone scan can miss purely lytic myeloma lesions. Get CT or MRI (or a skeletal survey). Myeloma is very radiosensitive, so even low palliative doses work well.

High-Yield Summary
  • In palliative care, the goal, the prognosis, and the stability of the bone or spine decide the plan, the way stage does in curative disease.
  • Performance status is the most useful predictor of survival, and clinicians tend to overestimate how long patients will live.
  • New back pain in a patient with cancer needs an MRI of the whole spine, and a bone scan can miss purely lytic lesions such as myeloma.
  • A SINS score of 7 or higher means a spine surgeon should see the patient, and mechanical pain suggests instability that radiation cannot fix.
  • A Mirels score of 9 or higher in a long bone means a high fracture risk and a referral for prophylactic fixation before radiation.

Palliative Radiation.title: Palliative Radiation
Palliative Radiation.html:
Palliative radiation answers one question: what is the shortest, simplest course that achieves this patient's goal? For most bone metastases the answer is shorter than students expect.

1
What is the goal?

Pain relief, local control, prevention of a fracture or cord compression, or durable control of limited metastases.

2
How long will they live?

Short survival favors a single fraction; long survival favors a longer course or SBRT.

3
Is it complicated?

Cord compression, a fracture or recent fixation, a soft tissue mass, or nerve pain change the plan.

The Fractionation Menu

For an uncomplicated, painful bone metastasis, these regimens give the same pain relief. About 60% of patients get meaningful relief and about a quarter become pain free. What differs is how many visits it takes and how often the pain comes back.

RegimenVisitsBest forTrade-off
8 Gy in 11Most uncomplicated bone metastases; poor performance status or short survival; patients who travel farAbout twice as likely to need retreatment (about 20% vs about 8%)
20 Gy in 55A middle ground; often used for neuropathic pain and cord compressionSlightly more acute side effects
30 Gy in 1010Longer expected survival, after surgical fixation, cord compression, or a large soft tissue massMost visits; no better pain relief for uncomplicated lesions
SBRT (for example 24 Gy in 2, 27 Gy in 3, 30-35 Gy in 5, or 16-24 Gy in 1)1-5Good prognosis, radioresistant tumors, oligometastases, some re-irradiationNeeds immobilization, MRI fusion, and image guidance; risk of vertebral fracture after spine SBRT
For an uncomplicated painful bone metastasis, 8 Gy in 1, 20 Gy in 5, and 30 Gy in 10 relieve pain equally well. The single fraction trades fewer visits for more retreatment.
RTOG 9714

In breast and prostate cancer bone metastases, 8 Gy in 1 relieved pain as well as 30 Gy in 10, with less acute toxicity and more retreatment.

Dutch Bone Metastasis Study

In more than 1,100 patients, 8 Gy in 1 matched 24 Gy in 6 for pain relief; retreatment was more common after the single fraction.

Reference: other bone metastasis trials▾
  • Chow meta-analyses: across randomized trials, single and multiple fractions give equal overall and complete pain response; retreatment is higher after a single fraction.
  • TROG 96.05 (neuropathic bone pain): 8 Gy in 1 could not be proven as good as 20 Gy in 5, so many clinicians use 20 Gy in 5 when the pain follows a nerve root.
  • ASTRO bone metastases guideline and Choosing Wisely: offer single fraction; avoid routine courses longer than 10 fractions for uncomplicated bone metastases.

What to Tell the Patient

  • Timing: pain usually starts improving in 1-2 weeks and is best at about 4-6 weeks. Keep taking pain medication until it does.
  • Pain flare: a temporary increase in pain within the first few days, in roughly a third to 40% of patients. Dexamethasone given around the treatment lowers the risk.
  • Side effects depend on the site: nausea when the field includes the stomach or upper abdomen, diarrhea for the pelvis, sore throat or swallowing pain for the cervical or upper thoracic spine, fatigue for most.
  • Retreatment is possible if pain returns.
NCIC SC.23

Dexamethasone 8 mg before and for several days after palliative bone RT reduced pain flare compared with placebo.

NCIC SC.20

For painful bone metastases needing re-irradiation, 8 Gy in 1 was noninferior to 20 Gy in 5 or 8 in the main analysis, with fewer side effects.

SBRT for Spine and Bone

SBRT gives a much higher dose in 1-5 treatments with tight margins. It is not needed for most palliative patients, but it helps when you need durable control: a good prognosis, a radioresistant tumor (kidney, melanoma, sarcoma), oligometastatic disease, or re-irradiation where the cord has already had its share.

SC.24

For painful spine metastases, SBRT 24 Gy in 2 gave more complete pain responses than conventional 20 Gy in 5.

RTOG 0631

Single-fraction spine SBRT (16-18 Gy) did not improve pain relief at 3 months over 8 Gy in 1, so SBRT is not automatically better for pain.

The main risks of spine SBRT are vertebral compression fracture (higher with lytic lesions, existing collapse, and very high single doses), pain flare, and rarely radiation myelopathy. SBRT needs MRI fusion, strict cord limits, and daily image guidance.

Prophylactic Radiation for High-Risk Bone Metastases

Most asymptomatic bone metastases are watched. But some are likely to cause a fracture, cord compression, or severe pain soon, and treating them early can prevent a hospitalization.

Gillespie (MSKCC, 2024)

In a randomized phase II trial, radiating asymptomatic, high-risk bone metastases (bulky lesions of 2 cm or more, hip, shoulder, or sacroiliac joint, junctional spine, or posterior vertebral involvement) caused far fewer skeletal-related events and hospitalizations, and patients lived longer, than standard care.

This is a phase II trial, so it is changing practice at many centers but is not a universal standard. The take-home: a bulky asymptomatic lesion in a weight-bearing or junctional site deserves a conversation, not just observation.

Reference: Gillespie trial details▾

Patients had widespread metastatic solid tumors with at least one high-risk asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic bone lesion. Skeletal-related events (pathologic fracture, cord compression, surgery, or radiation for pain) fell from about 29% to about 2%, hospitalizations for those events also fell, and overall survival at one year was better in the radiation arm. Larger confirmatory trials are under way.

Oligometastases: When Palliation Becomes Ablation

Some patients have only a few metastases. Treating each one with SBRT (with systemic therapy) may give durable control and, in selected patients, longer survival. This is a different goal from symptom relief, and it needs a different patient: good performance status, a controlled primary, and limited disease on modern imaging.

TermMeaning
OligometastaticLimited metastatic disease, usually up to 3-5 lesions
OligorecurrentA few new metastases after the primary was treated
OligoprogressiveMost disease is controlled on systemic therapy, but a few sites are growing; treat those and stay on the drug
SABR-COMET

In patients with a controlled primary and up to 5 metastases, adding SABR to standard care improved overall survival in a randomized phase II trial, with a small risk of treatment-related death.

ORIOLE

In oligorecurrent prostate cancer, SBRT delayed progression compared with observation; PSMA PET helped find all the disease.

NRG-BR002

In oligometastatic breast cancer, adding local ablative therapy to systemic therapy did not improve survival, a reminder that benefit is not universal.

Reference: other oligometastasis trials▾
  • Gomez: in NSCLC with up to 3 metastases after first-line systemic therapy, consolidative local therapy improved progression-free and overall survival.
  • STOMP: metastasis-directed therapy delayed the need for ADT in oligorecurrent prostate cancer.
  • CURB: SBRT for oligoprogressive disease improved progression-free survival in NSCLC but not in breast cancer.
  • Larger phase III trials (SABR-COMET-3 and -10 and others) are testing these results.

Other Palliative Targets

ProblemHow radiation helpsRepresentative regimens
Bleeding (bladder, cervix, rectum, lung, skin, stomach)Hemostatic RT often slows bleeding within a few days8 Gy in 1 (sometimes repeated), 20 Gy in 5, 30 Gy in 10
Airway obstruction or hemoptysisShrinks the tumor; a stent or bronchoscopic debulking is faster if the airway is critical17 Gy in 2 (a week apart), 20 Gy in 5, 30 Gy in 10; 10 Gy in 1 for poor performance status
Dysphagia (esophagus)Stent relieves faster; RT or brachytherapy is more durable20 Gy in 5, 30 Gy in 10
Head and neck massPain, bleeding, airway, and fungating tumorQuad shot: 14.8 Gy in 4 fractions over 2 days (twice daily), repeated every 4 weeks up to 3 times
Liver capsule painLow-dose whole-liver RTFor example 8 Gy in 1
Brain metastasesSRS, whole-brain RT, or supportive careSee the CNS module

Radiopharmaceuticals

When pain is everywhere, a drug that carries radiation to every bone metastasis can do what external beam can't.

AgentUseKnow
Radium-223 (alpha emitter, behaves like calcium)Castration-resistant prostate cancer with symptomatic bone metastases and no visceral metastasesALSYMPCA: improved overall survival, not just pain
Lutetium-177 PSMA-617PSMA-positive metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer after hormonal therapy and chemotherapyVISION: improved overall survival
Lutetium-177 dotatateSomatostatin receptor-positive neuroendocrine tumorsNETTER-1: improved progression-free survival
Strontium-89, samarium-153 (beta emitters)Diffuse bone painPain relief only; cause low blood counts

End of Life

  • Starting radiation in the last weeks of life is common and often more burden than benefit. If expected survival is short, give one fraction or none, and involve palliative care and hospice.
  • A short course should not delay hospice enrollment; many hospices can coordinate a single palliative fraction.
  • The most useful question in the room is often "What are you hoping this treatment will do for you?"

An 84-year-old with metastatic lung cancer, ECOG 3, lives 2 hours away and has a painful rib metastasis. Regimen?

8 Gy in 1. Same pain relief as longer courses, one trip. Retreatment is possible if needed.

A 52-year-old with ER-positive breast cancer and bone-only disease had a femur rod placed yesterday for an impending fracture. Regimen?

A multifraction course (for example 20 Gy in 5 or 30 Gy in 10) to the whole length of the hardware once the wound allows. Her prognosis may be years, and postoperative RT lowers the chance the rod fails.

A 60-year-old with renal cell carcinoma, a controlled primary, and a single painful T9 metastasis without cord compression, KPS 90. What do you consider?

Spine SBRT. Renal cell is radioresistant to conventional doses, and his prognosis justifies durable local control.

Three months after 8 Gy in 1 to a painful hip metastasis, the pain is back. Can you retreat?

Yes. Re-irradiation is common after a single fraction; 8 Gy in 1 again is reasonable (SC.20).

High-Yield Summary
  • For an uncomplicated painful bone metastasis, 8 Gy in 1, 20 Gy in 5, and 30 Gy in 10 relieve pain equally well, but retreatment is about twice as common after a single fraction.
  • Longer courses or SBRT make sense when the patient is expected to live a long time, after surgical fixation, for radioresistant tumors, or for limited metastatic disease.
  • Dexamethasone around treatment lowers the risk of a pain flare, and re-irradiation is possible when pain comes back.
  • The Gillespie trial showed that radiating asymptomatic, high-risk bone metastases prevented skeletal events and hospitalizations and improved survival in a phase II setting.
  • SABR-COMET showed that treating a few metastases with SBRT can extend survival in selected patients, while NRG-BR002 showed that the benefit is not universal.

Oncologic Emergencies.title: Oncologic Emergencies
Oncologic Emergencies.html:
True radiation oncology emergencies are few, but you will be paged about them. For each one, ask: is this actually a radiation emergency, or does something else (steroids, surgery, a stent, a biopsy) have to happen first?

EmergencyDo firstWhere radiation fits
Metastatic spinal cord compressionDexamethasone and MRI of the whole spineUrgent RT, or surgery then RT
Superior vena cava syndromeSecure the airway if needed, then get tissue; stent for severe symptomsAfter the diagnosis, for radiosensitive or chemoresistant tumors
Life-threatening bleedingResuscitate; endoscopy or interventional radiologyHemostatic RT when those fail or aren't possible
Airway obstructionBronchoscopy (debulking or stent) if criticalRT or brachytherapy for durable relief
Impending pathologic fractureProtect weight bearing; orthopedicsPostoperative RT after fixation
Symptomatic brain metastasesSteroids; neurosurgery for mass effectSRS or whole-brain RT (see CNS)
Before you radiate an emergency, ask what has to happen first: steroids, a scan, a surgeon, a stent, or a biopsy.

Metastatic Spinal Cord Compression

Up to about 5% of patients with cancer develop cord compression, most often from lung, breast, or prostate cancer, then myeloma, lymphoma, and kidney cancer. Most cases are in the thoracic spine.

Recognize It

  • Back pain is the first symptom in almost everyone, often for weeks before weakness. New back pain in a patient with cancer is cord compression until proven otherwise.
  • Then weakness, a sensory level, and finally bladder or bowel dysfunction (a late sign).
  • Ambulatory status before treatment is the strongest predictor of walking afterward. Patients who walk in usually walk out; patients paralyzed for more than a day or two rarely recover.
Cancer + back pain + a neurologic finding

Move fast: hours matter.

1
First,
Give steroids
Dexamethasone, commonly a 10 mg IV load then 16 mg a day in divided doses. Very high doses add side effects without clear benefit.
2
Then,
Image
MRI of the whole spine (many patients have more than one level). CT myelogram if MRI isn't possible.
3
Ask,
Is there tissue?
If this could be the first sign of cancer, a biopsy may be needed, but don't let it delay decompression.
4
Ask,
Is the patient a surgical candidate?
A single area of compression, a tumor that is not very radiosensitive, reasonable prognosis, and not paralyzed for long: surgical decompression and stabilization, then RT.
5
Otherwise,
Radiate
Urgent RT with steroids, started the same day if possible.
6
Consider,
SBRT
For radioresistant tumors with low-grade compression or a good prognosis, at experienced centers.
Patchell (2005)

In selected patients with cord compression from a single area of a non-radiosensitive tumor, direct decompressive surgery followed by RT kept more patients walking, and for longer, than RT alone.

SCORAD III

For cord compression in patients with a limited prognosis, 8 Gy in 1 gave ambulatory results close to 20 Gy in 5; it did not formally meet its noninferiority margin, but supports a single fraction for many patients.

Reference: more on cord compression▾
  • Patchell excluded radiosensitive tumors (lymphoma, myeloma, leukemia, germ cell tumors) and patients paraplegic for more than 48 hours. In the trial, 84% kept walking with surgery plus RT versus 57% with RT alone.
  • ICORG 05-03: 10 Gy in 1 was noninferior to 20 Gy in 5 for ambulatory status.
  • Retrospective series (Rades) suggest longer courses (30 Gy in 10) give better local control, which matters for patients expected to live longer.
  • Fields: conventional RT usually covers the involved vertebrae plus about one vertebral body above and below, and any paraspinal mass. After surgery, the field covers the operated levels and the hardware.

Superior Vena Cava Syndrome

Tumor (or a clot) blocks blood returning from the head and arms. Most cases are from lung cancer (especially small cell) and lymphoma; a growing share are from catheter-related thrombosis.

  • Symptoms: swelling of the face, neck, and arms, distended chest wall veins, shortness of breath, cough, and headache, all worse when lying flat or bending over.
  • Most patients are not in immediate danger, because collateral veins develop. The true emergencies are stridor or laryngeal edema and confusion from cerebral edema.
Severe symptoms
Stent first

An endovascular stent relieves symptoms within hours to a day or two. Radiation takes 1-2 weeks or more.

Stable patient
Diagnosis first

Get tissue before treatment. Small cell lung cancer, lymphoma, and germ cell tumors are treated with chemotherapy, and radiating before a biopsy can make the pathology unreadable.

Clinical Pearl

SVC syndrome used to be treated as an automatic emergency for radiation. Now the priorities are: protect the airway, stent if the patient is severely symptomatic, and get a diagnosis before you radiate.

Bleeding, Airway, and Fracture

1
Bleeding

Hemostatic RT (for example 8 Gy in 1, or 20 Gy in 5) works for many tumors, often within 24-72 hours. It complements, not replaces, transfusion, endoscopy, or embolization.

2
Airway

A tumor that is closing the airway needs a bronchoscopist first (debulking or stent). Radiation then keeps it open.

3
Fracture

A completed or impending fracture needs orthopedic fixation. Postoperative RT to the full length of the hardware improves function and reduces the need for repeat surgery.

A woman with breast cancer has had back pain for 3 weeks and now trips on stairs. Exam shows mild leg weakness and brisk reflexes. First two orders?

Dexamethasone and MRI of the whole spine, now.

A man with lung cancer has face and arm swelling for 2 weeks. He is breathing comfortably and is alert. CT shows a mediastinal mass. No biopsy yet. Radiate tonight?

No. He is stable, so get tissue first. If it is small cell or lymphoma, chemotherapy is the main treatment. A stent is the fast fix if he worsens.

A 55-year-old with renal cell carcinoma has a single-level T7 compression (Bilsky 3), has been weak for 12 hours, and can still walk with help. Best approach?

Surgical decompression and stabilization, then RT (Patchell). Renal cell is radioresistant and he is a good candidate.

A patient with myeloma has cord compression at T10 and can walk. Surgery or radiation?

Usually radiation. Myeloma is highly radiosensitive, so surgery is reserved for instability or bone fragments in the canal.

High-Yield Summary
  • For metastatic cord compression, give dexamethasone and get an MRI of the whole spine right away, because walking before treatment predicts walking after.
  • Fit patients with a single area of compression from a tumor that is not very radiosensitive do best with surgery followed by radiation, as shown by Patchell.
  • Patients with a limited prognosis can be treated for cord compression with a single 8 Gy fraction or 20 Gy in 5.
  • In superior vena cava syndrome, protect the airway, stent severely symptomatic patients, and get tissue before radiating, because small cell lung cancer and lymphoma are treated with chemotherapy.
  • Bleeding, airway obstruction, and fractures usually need a proceduralist first, with radiation adding durable control afterward.

Benign Disease.title: Benign Disease
Benign Disease.html:
Benign disease radiation uses doses so low they would never control a cancer. The skill is knowing which condition, at what stage, after which other treatments, and how to talk honestly about a small but real lifetime cancer risk.

ConditionGoal of radiationWhen it helps mostRepresentative regimen
Osteoarthritis (knee, hand, shoulder, hip)Pain reliefPainful joints that failed medicines, injections, and physical therapy, in older adults0.5-1 Gy per fraction, 3-6 Gy total
Plantar fasciitis / heel spurPain reliefChronic heel pain after conservative care fails0.5-1 Gy per fraction, 3-6 Gy total
Dupuytren disease (palm) and Ledderhose (sole)Stop progressionEarly: nodules or cords with little or no contractureAbout 30 Gy in two courses of 5 x 3 Gy, 6-12 weeks apart (or 21 Gy in 7)
Heterotopic ossificationPrevent bone forming in soft tissueHigh-risk patients around a hip replacement or acetabular fracture surgery7-8 Gy in 1, within 24 hours before or 72 hours after surgery
KeloidPrevent regrowth after excisionRecurrent keloids, started right after surgeryFor example 12-16 Gy in 3-4 fractions, within about 24-48 hours of excision
GynecomastiaPrevent breast growth on antiandrogensMen starting antiandrogen monotherapy (bicalutamide), before breast growthA single low dose (for example 10-12 Gy) with electrons
Graves orbitopathyReduce orbital inflammationActive, moderate disease, often with steroidsAbout 20 Gy in 10 (low-dose schedules also used)
Inflammatory conditions get a few Gy for pain. Overgrowth conditions get more, and must be treated early, before the scar, contracture, or bone has formed.

Safety First

1
Age

The lifetime risk of a radiation-induced cancer falls with age. Benign radiation is usually reserved for older adults; be very cautious under about 40.

2
Location

Keep the thyroid, breast, eyes, and gonads out of the field whenever possible. Hands and feet are relatively safe sites.

3
Consent

Explain the expected benefit, the alternatives, and the small cancer risk. Document it.

Osteoarthritis and Plantar Fasciitis

  • Who: older adults with chronic joint or heel pain that has not responded to NSAIDs, injections, physical therapy, orthotics, or weight loss, or who are poor surgical candidates.
  • How: very low doses, often 0.5-1 Gy two to three times a week, 3-6 Gy total, with a second course after about 6-12 weeks if the response is incomplete.
  • Side effects: essentially none acutely at these doses. Pain sometimes flares briefly before improving.
Dutch sham-controlled trials (Mahler, 2019)

In knee and hand osteoarthritis, low-dose RT (6 x 1 Gy) did not relieve pain better than sham radiation, a reminder that the placebo effect in joint pain is large.

Niewald (plantar fasciitis)

6 Gy (6 x 1 Gy) relieved heel pain better than a very low 0.6 Gy control dose, supporting a real effect in calcaneal pain.

The evidence is mixed: German series and some newer randomized trials report benefit, while sham-controlled trials have not always shown it. If asked, say that low-dose RT is an option after conservative care fails, with evidence that is still debated.

Dupuytren and Ledderhose Disease

Dupuytren disease is a fibroproliferative disorder of the palmar fascia: first nodules, then cords, then flexion contracture of the fingers (ring and little fingers most often). Ledderhose disease is the same process in the sole of the foot.

Early: nodules and cords, little or no contracture
Radiation

RT slows or stops progression in most patients by suppressing the proliferating fibroblasts.

Late: established contracture
Procedures

Needle aponeurotomy, collagenase injection, or surgery straighten the finger. RT can't reverse a contracture once the cord has matured.

  • Technique: low-energy X-rays (orthovoltage) or electrons to the nodules and cords with a margin of about 1-2 cm, with the rest of the hand shielded.
  • Regimen: about 30 Gy in two courses of 5 x 3 Gy separated by 6-12 weeks, or 21 Gy in 7 fractions.
  • Side effects: dry skin and mild redness acutely; late skin dryness, thinning, or reduced sweating in a few patients.
Clinical Pearl

The key word for Dupuytren is early. A patient who can still lay the hand flat on a table (a negative tabletop test) is the patient who benefits.

Heterotopic Ossification

Heterotopic ossification (HO) is bone that forms in soft tissue, most often around the hip after arthroplasty or acetabular fracture surgery, and around the elbow. It can cause pain and stiffness and sometimes needs another operation.

  • Highest risk: prior HO (the strongest predictor), ankylosing spondylitis, diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis (DISH), hypertrophic osteoarthritis, and male sex.
  • Why timing is everything: radiation kills the precursor cells before they turn into bone-forming cells, which happens in the first few days after surgery. Once bone has formed, radiation can't remove it.
  • Regimen: a single 7-8 Gy given within about 24 hours before or 72 hours after surgery; both work about equally well.
  • Shield uncemented (porous) prosthesis components so bone can still grow into them.
  • Alternative: NSAIDs such as indomethacin, which carry GI and kidney side effects.

Keloids

  • Keloids are scars that grow beyond the original wound. Excision alone often fails, frequently with a larger keloid.
  • Postoperative RT, started within about 24-48 hours of excision, lowers recurrence substantially.
  • Electrons or superficial X-rays (or brachytherapy) to the scar with a small margin; for example 12-16 Gy in 3-4 fractions.
  • Recurrence is higher on the chest, shoulder, and upper back (high-tension skin) than on the earlobe. Avoid in children when possible.

Gynecomastia Prevention

Men with prostate cancer who take an antiandrogen alone (for example bicalutamide) often develop painful breast enlargement. A single low dose to each breast bud before starting the drug prevents much of it. Tamoxifen prevents it even more effectively, and treatment after the breast has grown works poorly, because the tissue has become fibrotic.

Other Benign Conditions You May Hear About

ConditionWhere radiation fits
Graves orbitopathyOrbital RT for active, moderate disease, often with steroids; avoid in diabetic retinopathy; newer drugs (teprotumumab) have reduced its use
PterygiumBeta radiation (strontium-90 applicator) right after excision lowers regrowth
Desmoid tumorObservation or systemic therapy first; RT (about 50-56 Gy) for progressive or symptomatic disease when surgery would be morbid
Epicondylitis, shoulder syndromesLow-dose anti-inflammatory RT, similar to osteoarthritis
Benign tumors (meningioma, vestibular schwannoma, pituitary adenoma, paraganglioma)Fractionated RT or SRS; see the CNS module

A 70-year-old has painful nodules in both palms and can still lay her hands flat. Radiation?

Yes, she's a good candidate. Early Dupuytren disease: about 30 Gy in two split courses to slow progression.

A 64-year-old has a ring finger fixed at 60 degrees of flexion from a thick cord. Radiation?

No. RT can't reverse an established contracture. Refer for needle aponeurotomy, collagenase, or surgery.

A man with HO after his left hip replacement is scheduled for a right hip replacement next week. What do you offer, and when?

A single 7-8 Gy within about 24 hours before or 72 hours after surgery. Prior HO is the strongest risk factor.

A 25-year-old asks for radiation for knee osteoarthritis. What do you weigh?

Her age. The lifetime cancer risk is highest in young patients, and the evidence for OA pain is mixed. Other treatment is preferred.

High-Yield Summary
  • Osteoarthritis and plantar fasciitis are treated with a few Gy in small fractions for pain, although sham-controlled trials in osteoarthritis have questioned the benefit.
  • Dupuytren disease responds to radiation only in its early stage of nodules and cords, before a fixed contracture develops.
  • Heterotopic ossification is prevented with a single 7 to 8 Gy within about a day before or 3 days after surgery, and prior heterotopic ossification is the strongest risk factor.
  • Keloids are treated with radiation started within a day or two after excision, and gynecomastia must be prevented before the breast tissue grows.
  • Benign radiation is generally avoided in young patients and kept away from the thyroid, breast, eyes, and gonads.

Functional & Vascular Radiosurgery.title: Functional & Vascular Radiosurgery
Functional & Vascular Radiosurgery.html:
Radiosurgery isn't only for tumors. Two benign brain conditions come up again and again on the service and on exams: trigeminal neuralgia and arteriovenous malformations (AVMs). Both use a single, very precise, very high dose, and in both the benefit is delayed.

Trigeminal neuralgia
Target: a nerve

A tiny spot on the trigeminal nerve root gets 70-90 Gy maximum dose. Pain relief takes weeks to months.

AVM
Target: a tangle of vessels

The whole nidus gets about 16-25 Gy at its edge. The vessels close over 1-3 years, and the bleeding risk lasts until they do.

In functional and vascular radiosurgery, the effect is delayed. Pain relief takes weeks, and AVM closure takes years.

Trigeminal Neuralgia

Recognize It

  • Brief, electric shock-like, one-sided facial pain lasting seconds, usually in the V2 or V3 distribution (cheek, jaw).
  • Triggered by light touch, chewing, talking, brushing teeth, or wind. Between attacks the patient is usually pain free and the neurologic exam is normal.
  • Most patients are over 50 and more are women. In a young patient or with bilateral symptoms, think of multiple sclerosis.
  • The usual cause is a blood vessel (most often the superior cerebellar artery) pressing on the nerve where it enters the pons, wearing away its myelin.

Workup and First-Line Treatment

  • MRI with thin-slice sequences to exclude a tumor or MS and to look for a compressing vessel.
  • Carbamazepine (or oxcarbazepine) is first-line and works for most patients at first. Procedures are for pain that drugs no longer control or side effects the patient can't tolerate.
ProcedureBest forTrade-off
Microvascular decompressionYounger, healthy patients with a compressing vesselMost durable relief, but a craniotomy
Percutaneous rhizotomy (glycerol, balloon, radiofrequency)Older patients who want immediate reliefQuick, but more numbness and recurrence
Stereotactic radiosurgeryOlder or medically frail patients, those on anticoagulants, or after other procedures failNoninvasive, but relief is delayed and recurrence is common over years

Radiosurgery Details

  • Target: the trigeminal nerve root in the cistern, a few millimeters in front of where it enters the pons, with a single small (4 mm) shot.
  • Dose: a maximum dose of 70-90 Gy (often about 80 Gy) in one session. Because the target is a nerve, the dose is prescribed to the center, not the edge.
  • Response: most patients get meaningful relief, usually starting within about 1-3 months. About half are still pain free several years later; repeat SRS is possible.
  • Main side effect: facial numbness or tingling in a minority, more often with higher doses and retreatment. Severe painful numbness (anesthesia dolorosa) is rare.
Reference: Barrow Neurological Institute (BNI) pain score▾

Outcomes are reported on the BNI scale: I no pain, no medication; II occasional pain, no medication; IIIa no pain on medication; IIIb some pain, adequately controlled on medication; IV some pain, not adequately controlled; V severe pain, no relief. "Success" is usually BNI I-IIIb.

Arteriovenous Malformations

An AVM is a tangle of abnormal vessels (the nidus) where arteries connect directly to veins without capillaries in between. The high-pressure flow can rupture.

Recognize It

  • Hemorrhage is the most common presentation, usually in a young adult; then seizures, headache, or a focal deficit. Many are found by chance on MRI.
  • The risk of bleeding is roughly 2-4% per year, higher after a prior bleed and with deep location, deep venous drainage, or an associated aneurysm.
  • Catheter angiography is the gold standard to map the feeding arteries, nidus, and draining veins.

Spetzler-Martin Grade

FeaturePoints
Size: under 3 cm / 3-6 cm / over 6 cm1 / 2 / 3
Eloquent brain nearby (motor, sensory, language, visual cortex, thalamus, brainstem): no / yes0 / 1
Venous drainage: superficial only / any deep0 / 1

Grades run I-V. Low grades (I-II) are usually best treated with surgery, which cures immediately. Small AVMs in deep or eloquent locations, where surgery is risky, are the classic radiosurgery patients. High grades (IV-V) are often observed.

Radiosurgery Details

  • Who: small AVMs (usually under about 3 cm, or about 10 cc) in deep or eloquent brain.
  • Dose: about 16-25 Gy to the edge of the nidus in one session, often around 18-22 Gy. Higher doses close more AVMs but cause more brain injury.
  • How it works: radiation injures the vessel lining, which slowly thickens until the vessels close. Complete obliteration takes 1-3 years and occurs in roughly 70-80% of small AVMs.
  • The latency period: until the AVM is fully obliterated, the bleeding risk remains. Patients need to understand this.
  • Follow-up: MRI every 6-12 months, then angiography to confirm obliteration, usually around 3 years.
  • Side effects: imaging changes around the treated area are common; symptomatic swelling, seizures, or late cysts occur in a minority.
ARUBA

In unruptured brain AVMs, medical management alone led to fewer strokes and deaths over the short follow-up than medical management plus intervention (surgery, embolization, or SRS). The trial is widely debated, but it made observation a real option for unruptured AVMs.

Clinical Pearl

Ruptured AVMs are usually treated, because the risk of bleeding again is highest in the first year. For unruptured AVMs, the decision weighs a lifetime of small annual risk (higher in young patients) against the immediate risk of treatment.

Other Functional Radiosurgery

  • Essential tremor and tremor-dominant Parkinson disease: Gamma Knife thalamotomy (a very high single dose to the ventral intermediate nucleus) for patients who can't have deep brain stimulation or focused ultrasound. Effect is delayed by months.
  • Cardiac radioablation for refractory ventricular tachycardia (a single 25 Gy to the arrhythmia scar) is an emerging, investigational use.

A 72-year-old on warfarin has electric shock-like right jaw pain when she chews. Carbamazepine now makes her too drowsy. MRI shows no tumor. Which procedure fits her best?

Stereotactic radiosurgery. It is noninvasive, needs no stopping of anticoagulation, and suits an older patient; relief takes weeks.

What is the main side effect to counsel her about?

Facial numbness or tingling in the treated distribution, in a minority of patients.

A 28-year-old has a 2.2 cm AVM in the left thalamus with deep venous drainage that bled 2 months ago. Spetzler-Martin grade, and best option?

Size 1 + eloquent 1 + deep drainage 1 = grade III. Deep and eloquent location makes surgery risky, so SRS is a good option.

Six months after SRS, the AVM above is smaller but still fills on MRA. Is he protected from bleeding?

No. The bleeding risk persists until the AVM is completely obliterated, which usually takes 1-3 years.

High-Yield Summary
  • Trigeminal neuralgia causes brief, electric shock-like facial pain in the V2 or V3 distribution, and carbamazepine is the first-line treatment.
  • Radiosurgery for trigeminal neuralgia gives a maximum dose of about 70 to 90 Gy to the nerve root, relief starts within weeks to months, and facial numbness is the main side effect.
  • The Spetzler-Martin grade adds AVM size, eloquent location, and deep venous drainage, and small AVMs in deep or eloquent brain are the classic radiosurgery patients.
  • After AVM radiosurgery, the vessels close over 1 to 3 years, and the bleeding risk remains until obliteration is confirmed by angiography.
  • ARUBA found that medical management alone did better than intervention for unruptured AVMs over its short follow-up, which made observation a real option.

Other Sites in Brief.title: Other Sites in Brief
Other Sites in Brief.html:
These sites don't have their own module, but they appear on the schedule and on exams. For each one: where does radiation fit, and what is the one rule or trial to know?

Lymphoma

Lymphomas are very radiosensitive, so doses are low (often 20-36 Gy) and radiation is usually given after chemotherapy as consolidation. Fields have shrunk from large extended fields to involved-site RT (ISRT), which treats only the originally involved nodes, to cut late effects.

DiseaseWhere radiation fitsKnow
Early Hodgkin lymphomaShort chemotherapy (ABVD) then ISRT: 20 Gy for favorable disease, 30 Gy for unfavorableGHSG HD10/HD11 set those doses. PET-adapted trials (RAPID, H10, HD16): omitting RT after a negative interim PET slightly increases relapse but not death, so the decision is individualized.
Diffuse large B-cell lymphomaR-CHOP, then RT to bulky disease or a PET-positive residual mass (often 30-36 Gy)Early, low-risk disease can be treated with chemotherapy alone
Follicular lymphoma, early stageISRT 24 Gy alone can be curativeFORT: 24 Gy controlled disease better than 4 Gy
Indolent lymphoma, palliative4 Gy in 2 ("boom-boom") relieves symptomsVery low dose, high response
Gastric MALT lymphomaH. pylori eradication first; RT (about 24-30 Gy) if it persists or is H. pylori negativeHighly curable with RT
Mycosis fungoidesLocal RT for plaques; total skin electron beam for widespread skin diseaseEven single low doses work for individual lesions
Clinical Pearl

Why fields shrank: survivors of Hodgkin lymphoma treated with large mantle fields as young women had high rates of breast cancer, heart disease, and hypothyroidism decades later.

Skin Cancer

  • Basal and squamous cell carcinoma: surgery (often Mohs) is standard. Definitive RT is an excellent alternative for older patients and for the nose, eyelid, lip, and ear, where surgery would cost function or cosmesis.
  • Adjuvant RT after surgery for squamous cell carcinoma with perineural invasion of a named nerve, positive margins that can't be re-excised, or nodal disease.
  • Be cautious in young patients (late cosmetic changes), on the lower leg (poor healing), in genetic syndromes that sensitize to radiation (Gorlin, xeroderma pigmentosum), and in connective tissue diseases such as scleroderma.
  • Merkel cell carcinoma: aggressive and very radiosensitive; wide excision with sentinel node biopsy, then RT to the tumor bed (and often the nodes).
  • Melanoma: adjuvant nodal RT lowers regional recurrence without improving survival (ANZMTG/TROG); used less in the immunotherapy era. RT is common for melanoma brain metastases (see CNS).

Regimens range from about 50-60 Gy in 20-30 fractions to shorter courses (for example 35 Gy in 5 or 40 Gy in 10) for frail patients.

Soft Tissue Sarcoma

For extremity sarcoma, limb-sparing surgery plus radiation replaced amputation with the same survival. The question is whether to give radiation before or after surgery.

Preoperative
About 50 Gy in 25

Smaller field, lower dose, less permanent fibrosis, edema, and joint stiffness, but more wound complications. Now commonly preferred.

Postoperative
About 60-66 Gy

Fewer wound problems, but a larger, higher-dose field and more permanent late effects.

NCIC SR2 (O'Sullivan)

Preoperative and postoperative RT gave the same local control in extremity sarcoma; preoperative RT had about twice the wound complications, and postoperative RT more late fibrosis.

STRASS

In retroperitoneal sarcoma, preoperative RT did not improve abdominal recurrence-free survival overall.

Plasmacytoma and Myeloma

  • Solitary plasmacytoma (one lesion, no myeloma): definitive RT, about 40-50 Gy, controls the lesion in most patients, though many solitary bone plasmacytomas later progress to myeloma.
  • Multiple myeloma: radiation is palliative and very low doses work (for example 8 Gy in 1 or 20 Gy in 5). Keep fields small to protect marrow for future therapy and stem cell collection.

Pediatrics

Children are the most sensitive patients to late effects: growth, cognition, hormones, fertility, and second cancers. That is why pediatric plans use the lowest effective dose, often use protons, and young children often need daily anesthesia to lie still.

TumorWhere radiation fits
MedulloblastomaCraniospinal RT plus a posterior fossa boost after surgery (see CNS)
Wilms tumorLow-dose flank RT for higher-stage disease; whole-lung RT for lung metastases that don't resolve with chemo
RhabdomyosarcomaRT for most patients except completely resected, favorable tumors
Ewing sarcomaRadiosensitive; RT when surgery would be too morbid or margins are positive
Hodgkin lymphomaResponse-adapted: RT omitted for many children who respond well to chemotherapy

Total Body Irradiation

TBI is part of the conditioning regimen before some allogeneic stem cell transplants (most often for leukemia): it kills leukemia cells, including those in sanctuary sites, and suppresses the immune system so the donor graft can take. Myeloablative regimens give about 12-13.2 Gy in 6-8 twice-daily fractions; non-myeloablative regimens give as little as 2 Gy. The lungs are the main dose-limiting organ (pneumonitis), so they are often partly shielded.

Also on the Schedule

SiteWhere radiation fitsKnow
BladderTrimodality therapy (maximal TURBT, then chemoRT) as a bladder-sparing alternative to cystectomyBC2001: adding chemo to RT improved local control
Testicular seminoma, stage ISurveillance is preferred; para-aortic RT (20 Gy) or single-dose carboplatin are alternativesVery radiosensitive; low doses cure
ThymomaPostoperative RT for invasive or incompletely resected tumorsMyasthenia gravis is a common association
Uveal melanomaPlaque brachytherapy for medium tumors preserves the eyeCOMS: same survival as enucleation
Renal cell carcinomaSBRT for primary tumors in patients who can't have surgery, and for metastasesRadioresistant to conventional doses, but responds to ablative doses
High-Yield Summary
  • Lymphoma is very radiosensitive, so involved-site radiation uses low doses, usually after chemotherapy, and early follicular lymphoma can be cured with 24 Gy alone.
  • Radiation is an excellent alternative to surgery for basal and squamous cell skin cancers of the nose, eyelid, lip, and ear in older patients.
  • Preoperative radiation for extremity sarcoma causes more wound complications, while postoperative radiation causes more permanent fibrosis and stiffness.
  • A solitary plasmacytoma is treated definitively with about 40 to 50 Gy, while myeloma needs only low palliative doses.
  • Children are the most vulnerable to late effects, so pediatric radiation uses the lowest effective dose and often protons.
